(1) future doctors and future lawyers differ in the extent to which they favour giving information to patients with cancer; (2) future doctors favour giving information more often than future lawyers, and (3) future lawyers are more often in favour of giving information even if the patient does not request it, and they are more often in support of giving information to patients who do not wish to be informed than future doctors are.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how much information patients should be given about their diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment options, especially in the case of a cancer diagnosis.
the attitudes of medical and non-medical students to the question of whether a cancer patient should be informed about his or her diagnosis and prognosis.
the ethical issue of whether or not a physician should inform a cancer patient of his or her diagnosis and prognosis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
future lawyers and doctors differ in attitudes toward informing cancer patients about their diagnosis and their prognosis.
medical students are more in favour of informing patients of their diagnosis and prognosis than law students, and that law students are more in agreement with the principle of informed consent.
future physicians are more likely to be influenced in their attitudes toward truth telling by the patient’s wishes than future lawyers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the future lawyers and physicians have similar attitudes towards the right to know and the right to not know.
medical students and law students differ in their attitudes towards informing a cancer patient of their diagnosis and prognosis.

we have shown that the differences in attitudes according to case and type of study are related to convictions about benefit and harm of information, and the reasons given by the participants are helpful in considering means to achieve acceptance of the patients right to know and to not know.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the law and medicine should be more closely aligned when it comes to the issue of patient autonomy and disclosure of medical information.
the medical and legal communities are not on the same page when it comes to the issue of informing cancer patients about their diagnosis and/or prognosis.
there is a need for more research on the topic.
